analysis.one_liner: Makes every child and young adult under 26 eligible for Medicaid with automatic enrollment at birth.
analysis.headline: Six Democratic senators backed the bill when it was introduced in July 2026, and the Senate Finance Committee has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite Medicaid so that every child born in the United States is enrolled in the program automatically at birth and stays eligible until age 26, no matter their family's income. Coverage would be continuous, so no one in that age range loses it between paperwork renewals, and it would apply regardless of immigration status. Children with other qualifying insurance, such as a parent's employer plan, could opt out. The federal government would pick up 100% of the cost for people made newly eligible under the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: All children and young adults under 26, especially the uninsured: kids in low- and moderate-income families who don't currently qualify, young adults who lose their parents' plan or age off at 18, and children who are not lawfully present. Families would no longer have to prove eligibility or re-enroll, since enrollment is automatic and continuous.

how_it_helps.text: Makes all individuals under 26 eligible for Medicaid through a new eligibility category, beginning two years after enactment [S2].
Requires states to automatically enroll every child at birth, with an opt-out for families whose child has other coverage meeting Affordable Care Act essential-health-benefit standards [S2].
Extends continuous eligibility from age 19 to 26, so young people are not dropped from coverage between income recertifications [S2].

Requires states to cover eligible children and young adults regardless of immigration status, and bars the federal government from counting that care against their sponsors or passing the cost on [S2].
Pays states 100% of the cost of covering people who were not already eligible for full Medicaid benefits as of January 1, 2025, shielding states from the new spending [S2].
Extends comprehensive pediatric screening and treatment coverage (EPSDT) from age 21 to 26 and frees all under-26 enrollees from Medicaid work requirements [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would bear nearly all of the cost, since the bill requires the federal government to match 100% of spending on the newly eligible. States would keep paying their current share for people already eligible. The bill includes no taxes or spending cuts to offset the new outlay. Hospitals and insurers who lose patients' private coverage to the free public option would also bear a cost.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no financing mechanism: it creates what is likely one of the largest single health coverage expansions in decades with no revenue offsets, so the cost lands on the federal deficit [S2].
Because Medicaid pays doctors and hospitals less than private insurance, some families may see longer waits or narrower provider networks after moving children onto the program [S2].

Free automatic enrollment with a permissive opt-out could pull families who can afford private coverage onto the public program, shifting costs away from private insurers and employers and onto taxpayers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and direct: guaranteed, automatic, no-red-tape health coverage for every American from birth through age 25, including children who have never had a path to coverage. The cost is also large and unaddressed — the bill proposes the spending without any offsetting revenue, which makes it a much heavier lift even for legislators sympathetic to the goal. The design trade-off is that automatic free enrollment is simple for families but weakens the incentive to stay in private coverage. An honest supporter would acknowledge that this bill is a statement of principle more than a piece of legislation positioned to pass as written.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate on July 21, 2026 and referred to the Finance Committee, which has not held a hearing, taken a vote, or moved it any further.

narrative.text: Sen. Andy Kim introduced the MediKids Act in the Senate on July 21, 2026 [S1][S4].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, with no further action since [S4].
Five Democratic senators cosponsored the bill, all from the same party [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far no outcome has been reached. If the bill stays parked in committee, the status quo benefits private insurers and the federal treasury, while the uninsured children it targeted remain uncovered.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No final outcome yet; bill idles in committee

for.name: Sen. Andy Kim
for.what_they_did: Introduced the MediKids Act and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Sens. Tammy Duckworth, Alex Padilla, and Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Joined as cosponsors at introduction; named on the bill itself.

for.name: Two additional Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total cosponsorship to five, all Democrats.

sides.party_line_note: All six backers are Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored, and with the bill stuck in the Finance Committee without a hearing there is no roll call to show where the chamber's other senators stand [S3][S4].

industries.note: Most state Medicaid programs deliver care through private managed-care companies, so millions of automatically enrolled children would become paying enrollees for firms like these, locking in their role as the delivery channel. Their financial interest in this bill — more members, more revenue — runs in the same direction as the public's interest in covering kids.

industries.industry: Private health insurers (employer and individual market)
industries.note: The bill preserves families' right to opt out and keep employer or marketplace coverage, so most existing private plans are protected. But free automatic Medicaid invites families who can afford private coverage onto the public program, shrinking insurers' premium revenue and their risk pools over time.
Universal coverage for under-26s would sharply cut uncompensated care, since hospitals today absorb the cost of treating uninsured children. The trade-off is Medicaid's lower reimbursement rates.

analysis.trajectory: The bill faces long odds. It sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no hearing scheduled, has no Republican cosponsors, and contains no funding offsets — three strikes that typically mean a bill never reaches the floor before the 119th Congress ends in early January 2027. The likeliest path is that it dies in committee when the session ends, unless health coverage becomes a live negotiation topic or Democrats win chamber control in the November 2026 elections and revive it.
